sections.preamble: You are a coding assistant running inside pi, a coding agent harness. Help users inspect files, run commands, and modify code.
sections.tools:
<tools>
- read: Read file contents
- bash: Execute bash commands (ls, grep, find, etc.)
- edit: Make precise file edits with exact text replacement, including multiple disjoint edits in one call
- write: Create or overwrite files

Additional tools may be available.
</tools>
sections.rules:
<rules>
- Use bash for file operations like ls, rg, find
- Use read to examine files instead of cat or sed.
- You can inspect PI_* environment variables for current model and session details.
- Use edit for targeted changes. Batch changes to one file in a single call.
- Each edits[].oldText must exactly and uniquely match the original file. Keep matches short and non-overlapping; merge nearby changes without including large unchanged regions.
- Use write only for new files or complete rewrites.
- Be concise in your responses
- Show file paths clearly when working with files
</rules>

toolsAdded.name: read
toolsAdded.description: Read the contents of a file. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp, bmp). Images are sent as attachments. For text files, output is truncated to 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). Use offset/limit for large files. When you need the full file, continue with offset until complete.

path.description: Path to the file to read (relative or absolute)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read

toolsAdded.name: bash
toolsAdded.description: Execute a bash command in the current working directory. Returns stdout and stderr. Output is truncated to last 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever is hit first). If truncated, full output is saved to a temp file. Optionally provide a timeout in seconds.

timeout.description: Timeout in seconds (optional, no default timeout)

toolsAdded.name: edit
toolsAdded.description: Edit a single file using exact text replacement. Every edits[].oldText must match a unique, non-overlapping region of the original file. If two changes affect the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead of emitting overlapping edits. Do not include large unchanged regions just to connect distant changes.

path.description: Path to the file to edit (relative or absolute)

oldText.description: Exact text for one targeted replacement. It must be unique in the original file and must not overlap with any other edits[].oldText in the same call.

newText.description: Replacement text for this targeted edit.

edits.description: One or more targeted replacements. Each edit is matched against the original file, not incrementally. Do not include overlapping or nested edits. If two changes touch the same block or nearby lines, merge them into one edit instead.

toolsAdded.name: write
toolsAdded.description: Write content to a file. Creates the file if it doesn't exist, overwrites if it does. Automatically creates parent directories.

path.description: Path to the file to write (relative or absolute)

content.description: Content to write to the file

content.text:
# Instructions

Compute the result for a game of Hex / Polygon.

The abstract boardgame known as [Hex][hex] / Polygon / CON-TAC-TIX is quite simple in rules, though complex in practice.
Two players place stones on a parallelogram with hexagonal fields.
The player to connect his/her stones to the opposite side first wins.
The four sides of the parallelogram are divided between the two players (i.e. one player gets assigned a side and the side directly opposite it and the other player gets assigned the two other sides).

Your goal is to build a program that given a simple representation of a board computes the winner (or lack thereof).
Note that all games need not be "fair".
(For example, players may have mismatched piece counts or the game's board might have a different width and height.)

The boards look like this:

```text
. O . X .
 . X X O .
  O O O X .
   . X O X O
    X O O O X
```

"Player `O`" plays from top to bottom, "Player `X`" plays from left to right.
In the above example `O` has made a connection from left to right but nobody has won since `O` didn't connect top and bottom.

[hex]: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hex_%28board_game%29

####

Use the above instructions to modify the supplied files: connect.go
Don't change the names of existing functions or classes, as they may be referenced from other code like unit tests, etc.
Only use standard libraries, don't suggest installing any packages.
Do not modify the test files. Run the tests with: go test ./...

content.thinking: I need to look at the project structure to understand what we're working with.

Implement ResultOf. Parse the board lines (spaces are removed beforehand). For O, BFS from the top edge to the bottom edge; for X, BFS from the left edge to the right edge. Hexagonal neighbors in offset coordinates: after removing spaces, the rows form a parallelogram and each row has the same number of columns. Neighbor offsets: (0,±1), (±1,0), (1,-1), (-1,+1). Let me think about it for the parallelogram representation. Given the row indentation, do the cells shift to the right? Actually, the rows are indented, but after removing spaces they're just grids. Standard exercism solution: neighbors are {r-1,c}, {r-1,c+1}, {r,c-1}, {r,c+1}, {r+1,c-1}, {r+1,c}. This is standard.

Handle 1x1: X wins on a single X cell — a single cell connects left to right and top to bottom, so either one wins. Check O first, or check X first? Since the "X can win on a 1x1 board" test expects "X", "O" expects "O", both are fine — only one of the cells exists. If both O and X connected (which shouldn't be possible, but on an uneven board?), does exercism expect "X" if X wins first? Just check X first, then check O. Actually, typical solutions check both; per the game's rules, it should be impossible for both to win. Just check O? Order: if X wins, return X, otherwise if O wins, return O, otherwise return "".

Wait — about the neighbor offsets: for O's row indentation (where each row shifts one space to the right), do the cell (r,c)'s neighbors include (r+1, c) and (r+1, c+1)? Let me think. Visually shifting row r+1 one space to the right means its cell c is positioned below and to the right of row r's cell c. So (r,c)'s neighbors in row r+1 are (r+1, c-1) and (r+1, c)? Hmm. But the tests strip spaces anyway, and the standard exercism solution uses {1,-1} and {-1,1}… actually it varies. Both diagonal variants are transposes of each other, so as long as it's consistent, it doesn't affect connectivity. Either choice gives the same connectivity result for the whole group (since the board is a parallelogram, they're mirror images). No problem. Let's run the tests.

content.text:
All tests pass. Implementation summary:

**connect.go** — `ResultOf` does a flood-fill (DFS) twice:
1. **Player X**: seed the stack with all `X` stones in the leftmost column, then explore hex neighbors; if any reachable `X` touches the rightmost column, X wins.
2. **Player O**: seed with `O` stones in the top row; if any reachable `O` touches the bottom row, O wins.

Hex neighbor offsets in the offset-coordinate grid are `(0,±1)`, `(±1,0)`, `(1,-1)`, `(-1,+1)`. Returns `"X"`, `"O"`, or `""` when neither player has a connecting path.
